questions.question: Which of the following has unit volt-m$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
**(C) Electric field**

The electric field is $E=F/q$ (N C$^{-1}$) and also $E=-dV/dr$ (V m$^{-1}$). Since $1\ \text{N C}^{-1}=1\ \text{V m}^{-1}$, the unit volt per metre is that of the electric field.

Electric flux has unit N m$^{2}$C$^{-1}$, potential has volt, and capacitance farad.

questions.question: Electric field $(\varepsilon)$ and electric potential $(V')$ are related as:
questions.answer:
**(B) $\varepsilon=\dfrac{-dV'}{dr}$**

The electric field is the negative gradient of the potential: the field points from higher to lower potential, and its magnitude equals the rate of fall of potential with distance,

$$E=-\frac{dV}{dr}$$

Equivalently, $dV=-\vec E\cdot d\vec r$, so $V_B-V_A=-\int_A^B\vec E\cdot d\vec r$.

questions.question: If the distance between two plates of a parallel plate capacitor is doubled, its capacity:
questions.answer:
**(B) decreases 2 times**

For a parallel plate capacitor,

$$C=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$$

so $C\propto\dfrac{1}{d}$. If $d$ is doubled, the capacitance becomes half — it decreases by a factor of 2.

questions.question: If the temperature of a conductor increases, its conductivity:
questions.answer:
**(B) decreases**

The conductivity of a conductor is

$$\sigma=\frac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}$$

As temperature rises, the lattice vibrations increase, collisions become more frequent and the relaxation time $\tau$ decreases. Since $n$ is essentially constant for a metal, $\sigma$ decreases (equivalently, resistivity increases). Hence the conductivity decreases — and not linearly.

questions.question: If the length of a potentiometer wire is increased, the balance point will be obtained at:
questions.answer:
**(B) large length**

The potential gradient of a potentiometer wire is

$$k=\frac{V}{L}$$

so for a given emf to be balanced, $k\,l=\varepsilon$ gives $l=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{k}=\dfrac{\varepsilon L}{V}$. If the wire length $L$ is increased (same applied voltage $V$), the potential gradient $k$ falls, so a **larger length** $l$ is needed to balance the same emf. This also increases the sensitivity of the potentiometer, because a small change in emf then produces a bigger shift of the balance point.

questions.question: If the number of turns in a moving coil galvanometer is increased, its sensitivity:
questions.answer:
**(A) increases**

The deflection of a moving coil galvanometer is

$$\theta=\frac{NAB}{k}I$$

so the current sensitivity is

$$\frac{\theta}{I}=\frac{NAB}{k}\propto N$$

Increasing the number of turns $N$ increases the deflecting torque for a given current, hence the sensitivity increases (though the resistance of the coil also increases).

questions.question: The phase difference between current and voltage in an A.C. circuit containing capacitance only is:
questions.answer:
**(B) $90^\circ$**

For a capacitor, $V=V_0\sin\omega t$ and $I=C\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\omega CV_0\cos\omega t=\omega CV_0\sin\left(\omega t+\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Hence the current **leads** the voltage by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}=90^\circ$.

questions.question: Which of the following has smallest wavelength?
questions.answer:
**(D) $\gamma$-rays**

In the electromagnetic spectrum the wavelength decreases in the order

$$\text{radio}>\text{micro}>\text{IR}>\text{visible}>\text{UV}>\text{X}>\gamma$$

$\gamma$-rays have the shortest wavelength ($\sim10^{-11}$–$10^{-14}$ m) and highest frequency, hence the greatest penetrating power.

questions.question: In a white light spectrum produced by dispersion through a prism, the ray that is deviated least is:
questions.answer:
**(D) red**

Deviation by a thin prism is

$$\delta=(n-1)A$$

and since $n$ decreases with increasing wavelength (Cauchy: $n=A+\dfrac{B}{\lambda^{2}}$), red light has the smallest refractive index and therefore the **least deviation**. Violet, with the largest $n$, is deviated most.

questions.question: Dioptre is a unit for:
questions.answer:
**(C) power of a lens**

The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres:

$$P=\frac{1}{f\ (\text{m})}$$

Its SI unit is the dioptre (D); $1\ \text{D}=1\ \text{m}^{-1}$. A converging lens of focal length $1$ m has power $+1$ D.

questions.question: A plane wavefront is a part of a:
questions.answer:
**(C) both (a) and (b)**

A small portion of a spherical wavefront (far from a point source), or of a cylindrical wavefront (far from a line source), is very nearly flat and can be treated as a **plane wavefront**.

Hence a plane wavefront may be regarded as a part of either a spherical or a cylindrical wavefront at a large distance from the source.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: $1$ eV is equivalent to:
questions.answer:
**(C) $1.6\times10^{-19}$ J**

One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron when it is accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt:

$$1\ \text{eV}=e\times1\ \text{V}=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\times1\ \text{V}=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

questions.question: $1$ a.m.u. $(u)$ is equivalent to:
questions.answer:
**(B) $1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg**

The atomic mass unit is defined as $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of a carbon-12 atom:

$$1\ \text{u}=\frac{1}{12}\times\frac{12}{6.022\times10^{23}}\ \text{g}\times10^{-3}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$$

Its energy equivalent is $931.5$ MeV.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: The Boolean algebra for a NAND gate is:
questions.answer:
**(C) $\overline{A\cdot B}=Y$**

A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by a NOT gate, so its output is the complement of the product of the inputs:

$$Y=\overline{A\cdot B}$$

Its output is $0$ only when both inputs are $1$, and $1$ otherwise.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: In a semiconductor, electrical conductivity is due to:
questions.answer:
**(C) electrons and holes only**

In a semiconductor, current is carried by both the free **electrons** (in the conduction band) and the **holes** (vacancies in the valence band, which behave as positive charges).

The conductivity is

$$\sigma=e(n_e\mu_e+n_h\mu_h)$$

where $n_e$, $n_h$ are the electron and hole densities and $\mu_e$, $\mu_h$ their mobilities. This is why the Hall coefficient and thermoelectric behaviour of semiconductors are more complex than those of metals.

questions.question: What is electric flux? Give its unit.
questions.answer:
**Electric flux** linked with any surface is defined as the total number of electric field lines that pass through that surface. Analytically,

$$\phi=\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec S=\oint E\,dS\cos\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec E$ and the outward normal to the surface element $d\vec S$. For a closed surface enclosing charge $q$, Gauss's law gives $\phi=q/\varepsilon_0$.

**Unit:** The SI unit of electric flux is **N m$^{2}$ C$^{-1}$** (equivalently V m or J m C$^{-1}$).

questions.question: Give two differences between potentiometer and voltmeter.
questions.answer:
| Potentiometer | Voltmeter |
|---|---|
| Measures the emf of a cell very accurately. | Measures the emf of a cell only approximately. |
| Draws no current from the cell at balance (null-deflection method). | Draws some current from the cell, so it measures terminal voltage, not emf. |
| Sensitivity is high. | Sensitivity is low. |
| Based on the null-deflection method. | Based on the deflection method. |
| While measuring emf, the resistance of the potentiometer wire becomes effectively infinite. | While measuring emf, its resistance is high but finite (measurable). |

The essential point is that a potentiometer is a **null** instrument and therefore draws no current at balance, whereas a voltmeter must draw current to deflect, so it can never measure the true emf.

questions.question: What are isoclinic and isogonic lines?
questions.answer:
**Isoclinic lines:** Lines (curves) drawn on a map joining all places on the earth's surface having the **same angle of dip** (inclination) $\delta$. They are also called isoclinals. The line of zero dip is the magnetic equator, and the points of $90^\circ$ dip are the magnetic poles.

**Isogonic lines:** Lines drawn on a map joining all places where the **magnetic declination** is the same — i.e. where a magnetic needle deviates by the same angle from the geographic (true) north. The line of zero declination is called the **agonic line**.

questions.question: The core of a transformer is laminated. Why?
questions.answer:
The core of a transformer is laminated — made of thin sheets of soft iron insulated from one another rather than one solid block — in order to **reduce eddy currents**.

When the alternating flux in the core changes, it induces circulating (eddy) currents in the iron itself. These currents dissipate energy as heat, cause heating and noise, and reduce the efficiency of the transformer. Thin insulated laminations break up the eddy-current paths and greatly increase their resistance,

$$P_{\text{eddy}}\propto\frac{B^{2}f^{2}t^{2}}{\rho}$$

so the loss falls as the square of the lamination thickness $t$. Lamination therefore minimises energy loss and heating in the core.

questions.question: What is remote sensing? Mention two of its applications.
questions.answer:
**Remote sensing** is defined as obtaining information about an object or an area by observing it from a distance, without coming into actual physical contact with it. The sensors (cameras, radiometers, radars) are carried on aircraft or satellites and record the electromagnetic radiation reflected or emitted by the target; the data are then analysed to identify and measure the object.

**Applications:**

1. **In geology** — locating minerals, groundwater and oil, and mapping geological structures and faults.
2. **In agriculture (and forestry)** — crop-health and yield monitoring, soil-moisture estimation, detecting disease, and surveying forest cover.

(It is also used for weather forecasting, disaster and flood monitoring, and land-use mapping.)

questions.question: What is Rydberg's constant? Mention its unit.
questions.answer:
**Rydberg's constant ($R$):** Rydberg showed that the wave number of every line in the hydrogen spectrum can be written as

$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=\bar\nu=R\left[\frac{1}{n_1^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right]$$

where $\dfrac{1}{\lambda}=\bar\nu$ is the wave number and $n_1,n_2$ are integers ($n_2>n_1$). The constant $R$ appearing in this relation is called Rydberg's constant.

Its value for hydrogen is

$$R=1.097\times10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}=109677\ \text{cm}^{-1}$$

**Unit:** m$^{-1}$ (or cm$^{-1}$), since it multiplies a difference of reciprocal squares.

*(Equivalently $R=\dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}c}$, which follows from Bohr's theory.)*

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: What is LED? Mention two of its applications.
questions.answer:
**LED (Light Emitting Diode):** An LED is a specially designed forward-biased $p\text{–}n$ junction diode which emits light (a monochromatic beam of a required colour) when a current is passed through it. It is a substitute for the conventional incandescent lamp.

It works as follows: under forward bias, electrons from the $n$-region and holes from the $p$-region are injected across the junction. When an electron recombines with a hole at the junction, it falls from the higher to the lower energy level and the excess energy is emitted as a **photon** of energy $h\nu\approx E_g$. The colour of the light depends on the energy gap of the semiconductor (GaAs gives infrared, GaAsP gives red/yellow, GaN gives blue).

**Applications:**

1. Low operating voltage and low power requirement — used in indicator lamps, display panels, television screens and torches.
2. Used in optical communication, in remote controls, and for lighting; no warm-up time is required, unlike incandescent lamps or tubes.

questions.question: What is a signal? What are the different types of signal?
questions.answer:
A **signal** is information converted into an electrical (or electromagnetic) form that is suitable for transmission over a communication channel. Sound, pictures or data are first converted by a transducer into a voltage or current that varies with time.

**Types of signal:**

1. **Analog signal** — the signal level (voltage or current) varies continuously with time and can take any value in a range, e.g. the signal from a microphone. Such a signal has infinitely many values between two limits.
2. **Digital signal** — the signal level takes only two discrete values, high (1) and low (0), and changes in steps, e.g. the output of a computer. Digital signals are less affected by noise and are easily stored and processed.

$$\text{Message}\xrightarrow{\text{transducer}}\text{signal}\xrightarrow{\text{modulation}}\text{transmitted wave}$$

questions.topic: Electric Dipole in a Uniform Field
questions.question: Find a formula for torque acting on an electric dipole kept in a uniform electric field. Hence define electric dipole moment.
questions.answer:
Consider an electric dipole of charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $2a$, placed in a uniform electric field $\vec E$, with its axis making an angle $\theta$ with the field.

**Step 1 — Forces.** The force on $+q$ is $+q\vec E$ (along the field) and on $-q$ is $-q\vec E$ (opposite to the field). The two forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero — the dipole does not translate; they form a **couple**.

**Step 2 — Moment arm.** The perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces is

$$2a\sin\theta$$

**Step 3 — Torque.**

$$\tau=(\text{force})\times(\text{perpendicular distance})=qE\,(2a\sin\theta)=q(2a)E\sin\theta$$

Since the dipole moment has magnitude $p=q(2a)$,

$$\boxed{\tau=pE\sin\theta}\qquad\text{or vectorially}\qquad\vec\tau=\vec p\times\vec E$$

The torque is maximum ($\tau=pE$) when $\vec p\perp\vec E$ and zero when $\vec p\parallel\vec E$. It tends to align the dipole along the field.

**Electric dipole moment ($\vec p$):** It is defined as the product of the magnitude of either charge and the distance between them:

$$\vec p=q(2\vec a)$$

where the vector $\vec a$ points from $-q$ to $+q$. Its SI unit is coulomb-metre (C m); it is a vector quantity directed from the negative to the positive charge.

questions.question: What is drift velocity? Establish Ohm's law for conductors using idea of drift velocity.
questions.answer:
**Drift velocity:** The average velocity acquired by the free electrons of a conductor in the direction opposite to the externally applied electric field is called the drift velocity.

Let the drift velocity of the electrons be $v_d$, the conductor have length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$, and $V$ be the potential difference across it, with $E$ the electric field.

**Step 1 — Current in terms of drift velocity:**

$$I=neAv_d$$

where $n$ is the number of free electrons per unit volume.

**Step 2 — Drift velocity in terms of the field:**

$$v_d=\frac{eE\tau}{m}=\frac{eV\tau}{ml}\qquad\left(\because E=\frac{V}{l}\right)$$

**Step 3 — Substitute:**

$$I=neA\left(\frac{eV\tau}{ml}\right)=\frac{ne^{2}A\tau}{ml}V\quad\text{... (i)}$$

**Step 4 — Rearrange:**

$$\frac{V}{I}=\frac{ml}{ne^{2}A\tau}=\text{constant}=R$$

where the constant $R$, the resistance of the conductor, is

$$R=\frac{ml}{ne^{2}\tau A}=\left(\frac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}\right)\frac{l}{A}=\rho\frac{l}{A}$$

Thus $V=IR$ — **Ohm's law** — and the resistivity is $\rho=\dfrac{m}{ne^{2}\tau}$.

**Conclusion:** At constant temperature $n$, $\tau$, $l$ and $A$ are constant, so the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it. This establishes Ohm's law from the microscopic picture of drift.

questions.question: When a white ray of light passes through a prism, it is dispersed. Why? Why is red colour deviated least in a prism but violet colour is deviated most?
questions.answer:
**Why dispersion occurs:** The deviation produced by a prism is

$$\delta=(n-1)A$$

which depends on the refractive index $n$ of the material of the prism. According to Cauchy's relation,

$$n=A+\frac{B}{\lambda^{2}}$$

so $n$ depends on the wavelength of the incident light. White light consists of different colours of different wavelengths, so $n$ is different for each colour:

$$n_{\text{violet}}>n_{\text{red}}$$

Hence each colour suffers a different amount of deviation while passing through the prism, and the colours are separated — i.e. white light is dispersed into a spectrum.

**Why red is deviated least and violet most:** Red light has the **largest wavelength** ($\lambda_r\approx7000$ Å) and violet the **smallest** ($\lambda_v\approx4000$ Å). Since $n$ decreases as $\lambda$ increases (Cauchy's relation),

$$n_r<n_v\ \Rightarrow\ (n_r-1)A<(n_v-1)A\ \Rightarrow\ \delta_r<\delta_v$$

So the refractive index for red is least and for violet greatest, and consequently **red is deviated least while violet is deviated most**.

questions.question: What do you mean by coherence? How are coherent sources produced in laboratory?
questions.answer:
**Coherence:** Two sources of light are said to be coherent if they emit waves of the same frequency (same wavelength) and either in phase or having a constant initial phase difference, so that the phase difference at any point stays constant with time. Only coherent sources can produce a sustained (steady) interference pattern — for incoherent sources the phase difference varies randomly and the fringes shift and wash out.

**Production of coherent sources in the laboratory:**

1. **By division of wavefront:** A single wavefront is divided into two (or more) parts, which are then made to superpose at a small angle after travelling different optical paths. The two parts of the same wavefront act as coherent sources. Examples: Young's double slit (a plane wavefront divided by two narrow slits), Fresnel's biprism, Lloyd's mirror.
2. **By division of amplitude:** The amplitude of the incoming wavefront is divided into two or more parts by partial reflection and refraction at a surface; these parts are then superposed to produce interference. Examples: thin film interference (Newton's rings), Michelson interferometer.

Since both parts originate from the same source, they necessarily have the same frequency and a fixed phase relationship — hence they are coherent.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Find the energy of a yellow photon in eV. (Wavelength $(\lambda)$ for yellow light $=6000$ Å)
questions.answer:
Given: $\lambda=6000$ Å $=6000\times10^{-10}$ m $=6\times10^{-7}$ m, $h=6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$.

**Step 1 — Photon energy in joule:**

$$E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{6\times10^{-7}}$$

$$E=3.31\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

**Step 2 — Convert to electron volt:**

$$E=\frac{3.31\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}\ \text{eV}=2.07\ \text{eV}$$

**Answer:** The energy of the yellow photon is $3.31\times10^{-19}$ J $\approx2.07$ eV.

*(Handy shortcut: $E(\text{eV})=\dfrac{12400}{\lambda(\text{Å})}=\dfrac{12400}{6000}=2.07$ eV.)*

questions.question: What is radioactivity? Mention two properties each of $\alpha$-rays & $\beta$-rays.
questions.answer:
**Radioactivity:** Many unstable nuclei decay spontaneously into a nucleus of lower mass with a different combination of nucleons, emitting radiation in the process. This spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei is called radioactivity (discovered by Becquerel, studied by the Curies).

**Properties of $\alpha$-particles:**

1. An $\alpha$-particle is a helium nucleus, ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}^{2+}$, i.e. it carries two units of positive charge and has mass equal to four times the mass of a hydrogen atom.
2. It is deflected by electric and magnetic fields (towards the negative plate), has high ionising power but low penetrating power (stopped by a sheet of paper), and produces heating and can burn human skin.

**Properties of $\beta$-particles:**

1. $\beta$-particles are fast-moving electrons of nuclear origin; their charge and mass are the same as those of an electron (charge $-e$, mass $9.1\times10^{-31}$ kg).
2. They have ionising power less than that of $\alpha$-particles but much greater penetrating power, affect a photographic plate, and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields (towards the positive plate).

*(Emission of an $\alpha$-particle decreases $Z$ by 2 and $A$ by 4; emission of a $\beta$-particle increases $Z$ by 1 while $A$ stays the same.)*

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: Draw the circuit diagrams for $p$–$n$ junction diode as (a) half-wave rectifier, (b) full-wave rectifier.
questions.answer:
**Rectification** is the conversion of alternating current into direct current, done by a $p\text{–}n$ junction diode because it conducts appreciably only in forward bias.

**(a) Half-wave rectifier.** An a.c. source is connected through a transformer to a single diode in series with the load resistance $R_L$.

- During the positive half-cycle, the diode is forward biased and conducts, so the output voltage appears across $R_L$.
- During the negative half-cycle, the diode is reverse biased and does not conduct, so the output is zero.

Hence only one half of each cycle is rectified. The output is a pulsating d.c. whose frequency equals the supply frequency, $f_{\text{out}}=f$.

**(b) Full-wave rectifier.** Two arrangements are used: the centre-tap type (two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer) and the bridge type (four diodes).

- In a centre-tap rectifier, the two halves of the secondary are connected to two diodes which conduct in alternate half-cycles, each feeding the load in the same direction.
- In a bridge rectifier, during the positive half-cycle diodes $D_1$ and $D_3$ conduct, and during the negative half-cycle $D_2$ and $D_4$ conduct, so current through the load is always in the same direction.

Hence both halves of the cycle are rectified. The output frequency is double the supply frequency, $f_{\text{out}}=2f$, and the rectifier is more efficient ($\eta_{\max}=81.2\%$ against $40.6\%$ for half-wave).

questions.question: What are the different types of modulation?
questions.answer:
**Modulation** is the process of varying some characteristic of a high-frequency carrier wave in accordance with the instantaneous value of the modulating (message) signal, so that the message can be transmitted efficiently. There are three main types:

**1. Amplitude modulation (AM):** The **amplitude** of the carrier wave is varied in accordance with the amplitude of the modulating wave, the carrier frequency and phase remaining constant.

$$v=(V_c+m\sin\omega_m t)\sin\omega_c t$$

**2. Frequency modulation (FM):** The **frequency** (angular frequency $\omega_c$) of the carrier wave is varied in accordance with the instantaneous amplitude of the modulating wave, the amplitude remaining constant.

**3. Phase modulation (PM):** The **phase** $\phi$ of the carrier wave is varied in accordance with the instantaneous value of the modulating wave, keeping amplitude and frequency constant.

FM and PM are together called angle modulation. FM gives much better noise immunity than AM, which is why FM is used for high-quality music broadcast.

questions.topic: Equivalent Lens — Two Thin Lenses in Contact
questions.question: What is an equivalent lens? Find the equivalent focal length for a system of two thin lenses in contact.
questions.answer:
**Equivalent lens:** Two (or more) thin lenses in contact, behaving together as a single lens, are said to form an equivalent lens; its focal length is the equivalent focal length of the combination.

**Derivation:**

Let a point object $O$ on the principal axis of the two lenses (focal lengths $f_1$, $f_2$, in contact) be at a distance $u$ from the combination.

**Step 1 — First lens.** If the second lens were absent, the first lens would form the image $I_1$ of $O$ at distance $v_1$:

$$\frac{1}{v_1}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f_1}\quad\text{... (i)}$$

**Step 2 — Second lens.** Since the lenses are in contact, $I_1$ acts as the object for the second lens, which forms the final image $I$ at distance $v$:

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{v_1}=\frac{1}{f_2}\quad\text{... (ii)}$$

**Step 3 — Add (i) and (ii):**

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}\quad\text{... (iii)}$$

**Step 4 — Equivalent lens.** If the combination is replaced by a single lens of focal length $F$ which forms the image of $O$ at the same distance $v$, then

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{F}\quad\text{... (iv)}$$

Comparing (iii) and (iv),

$$\boxed{\frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}}\qquad\text{or}\qquad F=\frac{f_1f_2}{f_1+f_2}$$

In terms of power, $P=P_1+P_2$. If the lenses are separated by a distance $d$, the formula is modified to

$$\frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}-\frac{d}{f_1f_2}$$

questions.question: Distinguish between diffraction and interference. Discuss the diffraction of light due to a single thin slit.
questions.answer:
**Differences between interference and diffraction:**

| Interference | Diffraction |
|---|---|
| Superposition of waves from two (or more) **distinct** coherent sources. | Superposition of waves from the **same wavefront**, from different parts of the same aperture/obstacle. |
| Fringes are of **equal width** and equal intensity (for equal sources). | Fringes are of **unequal width**, and intensity falls off rapidly from the central maximum. |
| Maxima and minima are equally spaced and of the same intensity. | Central maximum is twice as wide and much brighter; the secondary maxima get progressively fainter. |
| Minima are perfectly dark (for equal amplitudes). | Minima are not perfectly dark. |

**Diffraction at a single thin slit:**

Let a parallel beam of monochromatic light from a source $S$ fall on a narrow slit $AB$ of width $d$ after passing through a convex lens $L_1$, and let the diffracted light be focused by a lens $L_2$ on a screen at distance $D$.

By Huygens' principle, every point of the slit $AB$ acts as a source of secondary wavelets. These wavelets superpose at a point $P$ on the screen making an angle $\theta$ with the normal, and the resultant intensity depends on the path difference between the wavelets from the two edges of the slit.

**Path difference between the extreme rays** from $A$ and $B$ is

$$\text{path difference}=d\sin\theta$$

**Minima:** If this path difference is an integral multiple of $\lambda$, the slit can be divided into an even number of half-period zones which cancel in pairs, giving

$$d\sin\theta=n\lambda,\qquad n=1,2,3,\dots\quad\text{(minima)}$$

**Maxima:** The secondary maxima lie approximately halfway between the minima:

$$d\sin\theta=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda,\qquad n=1,2,3,\dots$$

and the **central maximum** is at $\theta=0$ ($n=0$).

The intensity distribution is

$$I=I_0\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha}\right)^{2},\qquad \alpha=\frac{\pi d\sin\theta}{\lambda}$$

The central maximum is at $\theta=0$, has the greatest intensity and is twice as wide as the other maxima, whose intensity decreases rapidly with increasing $n$.

questions.question: State Ampere's circuital law. Find the magnetic field at a point inside a current carrying toroid. Hence find magnetic field at a point inside a long solenoid.
questions.answer:
**Ampere's circuital law:** The line integral of the magnetic field around any closed path in free space is equal to the absolute permeability $(\mu_0)$ times the net current passing through any surface enclosed by the closed path:

$$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$$

**Magnetic field inside a current-carrying toroid:**

An endless solenoid in the form of a ring is called a toroid. Let $r$ be its mean radius, $I$ the current through it and $n$ the number of turns per unit length. Take a circular closed path of radius $r$ inside the toroid (the field $\vec B$ has the same magnitude everywhere on it and is tangential, so $\vec B\parallel d\vec l$, $\theta=0^\circ$).

$$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\oint B\,dl\cos0^\circ=B\oint dl=B\,2\pi r$$

By Ampere's law, the current enclosed by this path is the current threading it, $(n\times 2\pi r)\,I$:

$$B\,2\pi r=\mu_0(n\,2\pi r)I$$

$$\boxed{B=\mu_0nI}$$

So the field inside a toroid is uniform in magnitude (independent of the radius of the toroid) and confined within it.

**Magnetic field inside a long solenoid:**

Consider a long solenoid of $n$ turns per unit length carrying current $I$, and take a rectangular path $ABCD$ with side $AB$ (length $l$) inside, parallel to the axis, and $CD$ outside the solenoid.

$$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\int_A^{B}+\int_B^{C}+\int_C^{D}+\int_D^{A}$$

- Along $BC$ and $DA$, $\vec B\perp d\vec l$, so the integrals vanish.
- Along $CD$, outside the solenoid, $B\approx0$, so that integral vanishes.
- Along $AB$, inside, $B$ is uniform and parallel to $d\vec l$, giving $Bl$.

$$\therefore\ \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=Bl\quad\text{... (i)}$$

By Ampere's law, the current enclosed by $ABCD$ is $n\,l\,I$:

$$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0 n l I\quad\text{... (ii)}$$

From (i) and (ii),

$$Bl=\mu_0nlI\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{B=\mu_0nI}$$

The field inside a long solenoid is uniform, axial and independent of the position within the cross-section.

questions.topic: Mutual Inductance of Two Coaxial Solenoids
questions.question: Find the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids.
questions.answer:
Consider two long coaxial solenoids $S_1$ and $S_2$, such that $S_2$ completely surrounds $S_1$. Let each have length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$, with $N_1$ and $N_2$ total turns respectively.

**Step 1 — Turns per unit length:**

$$n_1=\frac{N_1}{l},\qquad n_2=\frac{N_2}{l}$$

**Step 2 — Field of the inner solenoid.** Let a current $I_1$ flow through $S_1$. The magnetic field inside $S_1$ is

$$B_1=\mu_0n_1I_1=\mu_0\frac{N_1}{l}I_1$$

**Step 3 — Flux linked with one turn of $S_2$:** Since $S_1$ lies wholly inside $S_2$, this field passes through each turn of $S_2$:

$$\phi_2=B_1A=\mu_0\frac{N_1}{l}I_1A$$

**Step 4 — Total flux linkage of $S_2$:**

$$\Phi_2=N_2\phi_2=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2I_1A}{l}$$

**Step 5 — Compare with $\Phi_2=MI_1$:**

$$\boxed{M_{12}=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2A}{l}}$$

**Reciprocity:** Reversing the roles, a current $I_2$ in $S_2$ produces the field $B_2=\mu_0N_2I_2/l$ which links all $N_1$ turns of $S_1$, giving

$$M_{21}=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2A}{l}$$

Hence $M_{12}=M_{21}=M$ — the mutual inductance is the same in either direction. If the space is filled with a magnetic material of relative permeability $\mu_r$,

$$M=\frac{\mu_0\mu_rN_1N_2A}{l}$$

questions.question: "Lenz's law is in accordance with the law of conservation of energy." Explain. Find the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids.
questions.answer:
**Lenz's law and conservation of energy:** Lenz's law states that the induced emf (and hence the induced current) is always in such a direction as to oppose the cause that produces it — i.e. it opposes the relative motion or the change of flux that produced it.

Whenever there is relative motion between a coil and a magnet, a force begins to act which **opposes** the relative motion. Work must therefore be done by the external agent against this opposing force to maintain the motion, and this work appears in the circuit as electrical energy (and ultimately as heat).

- If the induced current were in the **same** direction as the change producing it (i.e. if the opposing force were an assisting force), the magnet would be accelerated without any external work being done, and electrical energy would be obtained for nothing.
- Since energy can neither be created nor destroyed, this is impossible.

Hence the induced effects must oppose the change, and the mechanical work done against the opposing force is exactly the electrical energy generated — Lenz's law is therefore a direct consequence of **conservation of energy**.

**Mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids:**

Let $S_2$ completely surround $S_1$; both have length $l$ and area $A$, with $N_1$ and $N_2$ turns.

$$n_1=\frac{N_1}{l},\qquad n_2=\frac{N_2}{l}$$

A current $I_1$ in $S_1$ gives the field

$$B_1=\mu_0n_1I_1=\mu_0\frac{N_1}{l}I_1$$

The flux linked with each turn of $S_2$ is $\phi_2=B_1A$, so the total flux linkage is

$$\Phi_2=N_2B_1A=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2I_1A}{l}\quad\text{... (i)}$$

But by definition $\Phi_2=MI_1$ ... (ii). Comparing (i) and (ii):

$$\boxed{M=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2A}{l}}$$

Similarly $M_{21}=\dfrac{\mu_0N_1N_2A}{l}=M_{12}=M$, so mutual inductance is reciprocal. With a core of relative permeability $\mu_r$, $M=\dfrac{\mu_0\mu_rN_1N_2A}{l}$.

questions.question: What do you mean by reactance and impedance in A.C. circuits? Prove that the average power dissipated in an A.C. circuit containing inductance only is zero. What is a choke coil?
questions.answer:
**Reactance:** The reactance of an a.c. circuit is the opposition offered to the alternating current by the inductance or the capacitance in it (or both). It is

$$X_L=\omega L\ \text{(inductive)},\qquad X_C=\frac{1}{\omega C}\ \text{(capacitive)}$$

and is measured in ohm. Reactance is frequency dependent and dissipates no power.

**Impedance:** The impedance of an a.c. circuit is the total effective opposition offered by the circuit (resistance together with reactance) to the alternating current:

$$Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_L-X_C)^{2}}$$

and the current is $I_{\text{rms}}=V_{\text{rms}}/Z$, with the phase difference $\tan\phi=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}$.

**Average power in a purely inductive circuit:**

Let the alternating current be

$$I=I_0\sin\omega t$$

In a purely inductive circuit the emf (voltage) leads the current by $\pi/2$:

$$V=V_0\sin\left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=V_0\cos\omega t$$

The instantaneous power is

$$P=VI=V_0I_0\sin\omega t\cos\omega t=\frac{V_0I_0}{2}\sin2\omega t$$

The average over a complete cycle is

$$P_{\text{av}}=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^{T}\frac{V_0I_0}{2}\sin2\omega t\,dt=\frac{V_0I_0}{2T}\left[\frac{-\cos2\omega t}{2\omega}\right]_0^{T}$$

Since $\omega T=2\pi$, $\cos(4\pi)=\cos0=1$, so

$$P_{\text{av}}=\frac{V_0I_0}{2T}\cdot\frac{-(1-1)}{2\omega}=0$$

(or simply $P_{\text{av}}=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi$ with $\phi=90^\circ$, so $\cos\phi=0$).

Hence the average power dissipated in a purely inductive circuit over a complete cycle is zero: energy is stored in the magnetic field during one quarter-cycle and returned to the source in the next, with no net dissipation. The average value of the alternating current itself over a complete cycle is likewise zero.

**Choke coil:** A choke coil is a device used in an a.c. circuit to oppose (reduce) the alternating current **without much loss of energy** — just as a resistance does in a d.c. circuit, but with negligible power dissipation. It is made by winding a thick insulated copper wire on a core of soft iron (or on a laminated core). Since it has a large inductance and a very small resistance, it offers a large reactance $X_L=\omega L$ to the a.c. but dissipates very little power ($P=I^{2}R$, with $R$ small). It is used for controlling current in fluorescent tubes and fans.
